arXiv:1404.4018v4 [math.AP] 19 Jun 2014

On the blow-up results for a class of strongly perturbed semilinear heat equations

V. T. Nguyen Email: vtnguyen@math.univ-paris13.fr Address: Université Paris 13, Sorbonne Paris Cité,
LAGA, CNRS (UMR 7539), F-93430, Villetaneuse, France.
Abstract

We consider in this work some class of strongly perturbed for the semilinear heat equation with Sobolev sub-critical power nonlinearity. We first derive a Lyapunov functional in similarity variables and then use it to derive the blow-up rate. We also classify all possible asymptotic behaviors of the solution when it approaches to singularity. Finally, we describe precisely the blow-up profiles corresponding to these behaviors.

Keywords: 
Finite-time blow-up , asymptotic behavior of solutions , nonlinear parabolic equations.

1 Introduction

We are interested in the following nonlinear parabolic equation:

{ut=Δ​u+|u|p−1​u+h⁡(u),u⁡(0)=u0∈L∞​(ℝn),\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}&=&\Delta u+|u|^{p-1}u+h(u),\\ u(0)&=&u_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),\end{array}\right. (1)

where uu is defined for (x,t)∈ℝn×[0,T)(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T), pp is a sub-critical nonlinearity,

1<p,(n−2)​p<n+2.1<p,\quad(n-2)p<n+2. (2)

The function hh is in 𝒞1​(ℝ,ℝ)\mathcal{C}^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) satisfying

j=0,1,|h(j)​(z)|≤M⁡(|z|p−jloga⁡(2+z2)+1),|h′′​(z)|≤M​|z|p−2loga⁡(2+z2),j=0,1,\;|h^{(j)}(z)|\leq M\left(\dfrac{|z|^{p-j}}{\log^{a}(2+z^{2})}+1\right),\quad|h^{\prime\prime}(z)|\leq M\dfrac{|z|^{p-2}}{\log^{a}(2+z^{2})}, (3)

where a>1a>1, M>0M>0. Typically, h⁡(z)=μ​|z|p−1​zloga⁡(2+z2)h(z)=\frac{\mu|z|^{p-1}z}{\log^{a}(2+z^{2})} with μ∈ℝ\mu\in\mathbb{R}.

By standard results, the problem (1) has a unique classical solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) in L∞​(ℝn)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), which exists at least for small times. The solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) may develop singularities in some finite time. We say that a function u:ℝn×[0,T)↦ℝu:\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T)\mapsto\mathbb{R} is a solution of (1) if uu solves (1) and satisfies

u,ut,∇u,∇2u​are bounded and continuous on​ℝn×[0,τ],∀τ<T.u,u_{t},\nabla u,\nabla^{2}u\;\text{are bounded and continuous on}\;\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,\tau],\;\forall\tau<T. (4)

It is said that u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) blows up in a finite time T<+∞T<+\infty if u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) satisfies (1), (4) and

limt→T‖u⁡(t)‖L∞​(ℝn)=+∞.\lim_{t\to T}\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}=+\infty.

Here we call TT the blow-up time of u⁡(x,t)u(x,t). In such a blow-up case, a point x0∈ℝnx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is called a blow-up point of u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) if and only if there exist (xn,tn)→(x0,T)(x_{n},t_{n})\to(x_{0},T) such that |u⁡(xn,tn)|→+∞|u(x_{n},t_{n})|\to+\infty as n→+∞n\to+\infty.

Consider vv a positive blow-up solution of the associated ODE of (1). It is clear that vv is given by

v′=vp+h(v),v(T)=+∞,for some T>0.v^{\prime}=v^{p}+h(v),\quad v(T)=+\infty,\quad\text{for some $T>0$.} (5)

Since the blow-up solution of (5) satisfies (see Lemma A.1)

v⁡(t)∼κ​(T−t)−1p−1as t→T, where κ=(p−1)−1p−1,v(t)\sim\kappa(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\quad\text{as $t\to T$, where $\kappa=(p-1)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}$}, (6)

it is natural to ask whether the blow-up solution u⁡(t)u(t) of (1) has the same blow-up rate as v⁡(t)v(t) does. More precisely, are there constants c,C>0c,C>0 such that

c​(T−t)−1p−1≤‖u⁡(t)‖L∞​(ℝn)≤C​(T−t)−1p−1,∀t∈(0,T)​?c(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\leq\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq C(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}},\quad\forall t\in(0,T)? (7)

By a simple argument based on Duhamel’s formula, we can show that the lower bound in (7) is always satisfied (see [19]). For the upper blow-up rate estimate, it is much less simple and requires more work. Practically, we define for all x0∈ℝnx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} (x0x_{0} may be a blow-up point of uu or not) the following similarity variables introduced in Giga and Kohn [4, 5, 6]:

y=x−x0T−t,s=−log⁡(T−t),wx0,T=(T−t)1p−1​u​(x,t).y=\frac{x-x_{0}}{\sqrt{T-t}},\quad s=-\log(T-t),\quad w_{x_{0},T}=(T-t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}u(x,t). (8)

Hence wx0,Tw_{x_{0},T} satisfies for all s≥−log⁡Ts\geq-\log{T} and for all y∈ℝny\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:

∂swx0,T=1ρdiv(ρ∇wx0,T)−wx0,Tp−1+|wx0,T|p−1wx0,T+e−p​sp−1h(esp−1wx0,T),\partial_{s}w_{x_{0},T}=\frac{1}{\rho}\text{div}(\rho\nabla w_{x_{0},T})-\frac{w_{x_{0},T}}{p-1}+|w_{x_{0},T}|^{p-1}w_{x_{0},T}+e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}w_{x_{0},T}\right), (9)

where

ρ⁡(y)=(14​π)n/2​e−|y|24.\rho(y)=\left(\frac{1}{4\pi}\right)^{n/2}e^{-\frac{|y|^{2}}{4}}. (10)

Here, we say that w:ℝn×[−logT,+∞)↦ℝw:\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[-\log T,+\infty)\mapsto\mathbb{R} is a solution of (9) if ww solves (9) and satisfies

w,ws,∇w,∇2w​are bounded and continuous on​ℝn×[−log⁡T,S],∀S<+∞.w,w_{s},\nabla w,\nabla^{2}w\;\text{are bounded and continuous on}\;\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[-\log T,S],\;\forall S<+\infty. (11)

We can see that the study of uu in the neighborhood of (x0,T)(x_{0},T) is equivalent to the study of the long-time behavior of wx0,Tw_{x_{0},T} and each result for uu has an equivalent formulation in term of wx0,Tw_{x_{0},T}. In particular, the proof of the upper bound in (7) is now equivalent to showing that there exists a time s^≥−log⁡T\hat{s}\geq-\log T large enough such that

‖wx0,T​(s)‖L∞​(ℝn)≤C,∀s≥s^.\|w_{x_{0},T}(s)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq C,\quad\forall s\geq\hat{s}. (12)

We remark that the perturbation term added to equation (9) satisfies the following inequality,

j=0,1,e−(p−j)​sp−1​|h(j)​(esp−1​z)|≤C0sa​(|z|p−j+1),∀s≥s0,j=0,1,\quad e^{-\frac{(p-j)s}{p-1}}\left|h^{(j)}\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}z\right)\right|\leq\frac{C_{0}}{s^{a}}\left(|z|^{p-j}+1\right),\quad\forall s\geq s_{0}, (13)

for some C0>0C_{0}>0 and s0>0s_{0}>0 (see Lemma A.2 for a proof of this fact).

When h≡0h\equiv 0, Giga and Kohn proved (12) in [5] for 1<p<3​n+83​n−41<p<\frac{3n+8}{3n-4} or for non-negative initial data (so that the solution is positive everywhere) with sub-critical pp. Estimate (12) is extended for all pp satisfying (2) without assuming non-negativity for initial data u0u_{0} by Giga, Matsui and Sasayama in [7]. The proof written in [7] is strongly based on the existence of the following Lyapunov functional:

ℰ0​[w]​(s)=∫ℝn(12​|∇w|2+12​(p−1)​|w|2−1p+1​|w|p+1)​ρ​𝑑y.\mathcal{E}_{0}[w](s)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\left(\frac{1}{2}|\nabla w|^{2}+\frac{1}{2(p-1)}|w|^{2}-\frac{1}{p+1}|w|^{p+1}\right)\rho dy. (14)

Based on this functional, some energy estimates related to this structure and a bootstrap argument given in [14], the authors in [7] have established the following key integral estimate

sups≥s′∫ss+1‖wx0,T​(s)‖Lp+1​(𝐁R)(p+1)​q​𝑑s≤Cq,s′,∀q≥2,s′>−log⁡T.\sup_{s\geq s^{\prime}}\int_{s}^{s+1}\|w_{x_{0},T}(s)\|_{L^{p+1}(\mathbf{B}_{R})}^{(p+1)q}ds\leq C_{q,s^{\prime}},\quad\forall q\geq 2,\quad s^{\prime}>-\log T. (15)

Since this estimate holds for all q≥2q\geq 2, we obtain an upper bound for wx0,Tw_{x_{0},T} which yields (12).

‖wx0,T​(y,s)‖L∞​(ℝn)≤C,\|w_{x_{0},T}(y,s)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq C, (19)

where wx0,Tw_{x_{0},T} is defined in (8) and CC is a positive constant depending only on n,p,Mn,p,M and a bound of ‖wx0,T​(s^0)‖L∞\|w_{x_{0},T}(\hat{s}_{0})\|_{L^{\infty}}.
(i​i)(ii) For all t∈[t1,T)t\in[t_{1},T) where t1=T−e−s′t_{1}=T-e^{-s^{\prime}},

‖u⁡(x,t)‖L∞​(ℝn)≤C​(T−t)−1p−1.\|u(x,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq C(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}. (20)
Remark 1.

The proof of Theorem 2 is far from being a straightforward adaptation of [7]. Indeed, three major difficulties arise in our case and make the heart of our contribution:
- the existence of a Lyapunov functional in similarity variables (see Theorem 1 above),
- the control of the L2L^{2}-norm in terms of the energy (see (i​i)(ii) of Proposition 8, where we rely on a new blow-up criterion greatly simplifying the approach in [5]),
- the proof of a nonlinear parabolic result (see Proposition 12 below).

The estimate obtained in Theorem 2 is a fundamental step in studying the asymptotic behavior of blow-up solutions. When h≡0h\equiv 0, Giga and Kohn in [5, 6] (see also [4]) obtained the following result: For a given blow-up point x0x_{0}, it holds that

lims→+∞wx0,T​(y,s)=limt→T(T−t)1p−1​u​(x0+y​T−t,t)=±κ,\lim_{s\to+\infty}w_{x_{0},T}(y,s)=\lim_{t\to T}(T-t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}u(x_{0}+y\sqrt{T-t},t)=\pm\kappa,

where κ=(p−1)1p−1\kappa=(p-1)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}, uniformly on compact subsets of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. The result is pointwise in x0x_{0}. Besides, for a.e. yy, lims→+∞∇wx0,T​(y,s)=0\lim_{s\to+\infty}\nabla w_{x_{0},T}(y,s)=0.

For our problem, when h≢0h\not\equiv 0 and hh is given in (3), we also derive an analogous result on the behavior of wx0,Tw_{x_{0},T} as s→+∞s\to+\infty. We claim the following:

Theorem 3 (Behavior of wx0,Tw_{x_{0},T} as s→+∞s\to+\infty).

Let a,p,n,Ma,p,n,M be fixed, pp satisfy (2). Consider u⁡(t)u(t) a solution of equation (1) which blows up at time TT and x0x_{0} a blow-up point. Then

limt→T(T−t)1p−1​u​(x0+y​T−t,t)=lims→+∞wx0,T​(y,s)=±κ,\lim_{t\to T}(T-t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}u(x_{0}+y\sqrt{T-t},t)=\lim_{s\to+\infty}\,w_{x_{0},T}(y,s)=\pm\kappa,

holds in Lρ2L^{2}_{\rho} (Lρ2L^{2}_{\rho} is the weighted L2L^{2} space associated with the weight ρ\rho (10)), and also uniformly on each compact subset of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Up to changing u0u_{0} in −u0-u_{0} and hh in −h-h, we may assume that w→κw\to\kappa in Lρ2L^{2}_{\rho} as s→+∞s\to+\infty. Let us consider ϕ\phi a positive solution of the associated ordinary differential equation of equation (9)

ϕs=−ϕp−1+ϕp+e−p​sp−1​h​(esp−1​ϕ)\phi_{s}=-\frac{\phi}{p-1}+\phi^{p}+e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\phi\right) (21)

such that

ϕ⁡(s)=κ+𝒪⁡(1sa)ass→+∞,\phi(s)=\kappa+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{a}}\right)\quad\text{as}\quad s\to+\infty, (22)

(see Lemma A.3 for a proof of the existence of ϕ\phi).
Let us introduce vx0,T=wx0,T−ϕ⁡(s)v_{x_{0},T}=w_{x_{0},T}-\phi(s), then ‖vx0,T​(y,s)‖Lρ2→0\|v_{x_{0},T}(y,s)\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}\to 0 as s→+∞s\to+\infty and vx0,Tv_{x_{0},T} (or vv for simplicity) satisfies the following equation:

Remark 2.

Applying our result to a space-independent solution of (9), we get the uniqueness of the solution of the ODE (21) that converges to κ\kappa as s→+∞s\to+\infty.

Remark 3.

Since both the perturbed (h≢0h\not\equiv 0) and the unperturbed (h≡0h\equiv 0) cases in equation (1) share the same convergence stated in Theorem 4, we wonder whether the perturbation hh may have an influence on further terms of the expansion of ww. From our result, if case (i​i)(ii) occurs, we see no difference in the following term of the expansion. On the contrary, if case (i)(i) or (i​i​i)(iii) occurs, with h⁡(x)=μ​|x|p−1​xlog⁡(2+x2)h(x)=\mu\frac{|x|^{p-1}x}{\log(2+x^{2})}, we see from Lemma A.3 that

w⁡(y,s)−κ∼C0​(a,p,μ)saas s→+∞,w(y,s)-\kappa\sim\frac{C_{0}(a,p,\mu)}{s^{a}}\quad\text{as $s\to+\infty$},

which is clearly different from the unperturbed case when in case (i)(i), we have w≡κw\equiv\kappa and case (i​i​i)(iii), we have w−κ=𝒪⁡(e−s)w-\kappa=\mathcal{O}(e^{-s}), (see [10], [18]).

Remark 4.

If we linearize ww around κ\kappa, which is an explicit profile, we then fall in logarithmic scales μ=1|log⁡ϵ|\mu=\frac{1}{|\log\epsilon|} with ϵ=T−t\epsilon=T-t. Further refinements in this direction should give an expansion of w−κw-\kappa in terms of powers of μ\mu, i.e in logarithmic scales of ϵ\epsilon. Therefore, we can not reach significantly small error terms in the expansion of the solution ww as (i​i​i)(iii) of Theorem 4 describes. In order to escape this situation, a relevant approximation is required in order to go beyond all logarithmic scales, i.e approximations up to lower order terms such as ϵα\epsilon^{\alpha} for some α>0\alpha>0. Our idea to capture such relevant terms is to abandon the explicit profile obtained as a first order approximation, namely κ\kappa, and take an implicit profile function as a first order description of the singular behavior, namely ϕ⁡(s)\phi(s) introduced in (21) and (22). A similar idea was used by Zaag [20] where the solution was linearized around a less explicit profile function in order to go beyond all logarithmic scales. For our problem, we particularly take ϕ⁡(s)\phi(s) as the implicit profile function, which is a solution of the associated ODE of equation (9) in ww such that ϕ⁡(s)→κ\phi(s)\to\kappa as s→+∞s\to+\infty. By linearizing the solution ww around ϕ\phi, we can get to error terms of polynomial order ϵ(m2−1)\epsilon^{\left(\frac{m}{2}-1\right)}, as stated in (i​i​i)(iii) of Theorem 4.

Remark 5.

Let us mention briefly the structure of the paper. In Section 2, we prove the existence of Lyapunov functional for equation (9) (Theorem 1), we then get Theorem 2 and Theorem 3. In Section 3, we follow the method of [3] and [18] to prove Theorem 4. Finally, the section 4 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 5.

2 A Lyapunov functional

This section is divided in four subsections: we first prove the existence of a Lyapunov functional for equation (9) (Theorem 1); after that, we derive a blow-up criterion for equation (9) and some energy estimates based on this Lyapunov functional. Following the method of [7], we prove the boundedness of solution in similarity variables which determines the blow-up rate for solution of (1) (Theorem 2). Finally, we derive the limit of ww as s→+∞s\to+\infty, which concludes Theorem 3.

This section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 2, which is a direct consequence of the following theorem:

Let a,p,n,Ma,p,n,M be fixed, pp satisfy (2). There exists s^1=s^1​(a,p,n,M)≥s^0\hat{s}_{1}=\hat{s}_{1}(a,p,n,M)\geq\hat{s}_{0} such that if uu is a blow-up solution of equation (1) with a blow-up time TT, then for all s≥s′=max⁡{s^1,−log⁡T}s\geq s^{\prime}=\max\{\hat{s}_{1},-\log T\},

2.4 Limit of ww as s→+∞s\to+\infty

This section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 3. Note in the unperturbed case (h≡0h\equiv 0) that Theorem 3 was proved in [6] (see also [4], [5]). The proof is divided into two steps. The first step is to show that the limit of solution in similarity variables exists and belongs to the set of solutions of the following equation,

0=Δ​w−12​y.∇w−1p−1​w+|w|p−1​w,0=\Delta w-\frac{1}{2}y.\nabla w-\frac{1}{p-1}w+|w|^{p-1}w, (50)

Then, by using a nondegeneracy result (Lemma 19), the blow-up criterion (Lemma 7) and suitable energy arguments, we shall show that the possibility of wa→0w_{a}\to 0 as s→+∞s\to+\infty is excluded if aa is a blow-up point. Let us restate Theorem 3 in below:

Proposition 16 (Limit of ww as s→+∞s\to+\infty).

Let a,p,n,Ma,p,n,M be fixed, pp be a sub-critical non-linearity given in (2). Consider u⁡(t)u(t) a solution of equation (1) which blows up at time TT and aa a blow-up point. Then

lims→+∞wa​(y,s)=±κ,uniformly on each compact subset of ℝn.\lim_{s\to+\infty}\,w_{a}(y,s)=\pm\kappa,\quad\text{uniformly on each compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.}

Before going into the proof of Proposition 16, let us first derive some elementary results. The first one concerns the stationary solutions in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} of equation (50). Particularly, we have the following:

Lemma 17 (Stationary solutions, Giga and Kohn [4]).

Let pp satisfy (2), then all bounded solutions of (50) are constants: w≡0w\equiv 0 or w≡±κw\equiv\pm\kappa.

Proof.

The proof is given in Proposition 2 of [4]. For the reader’s interest, we mention that the proof relies on a clever use of multiplying factors, together with a Pohozaev technique, resulting in the following identity:

(np+1−2−n2)​∫ℝn|∇w|2​ρ​𝑑y+12​(12−1p+1)​∫ℝn|y|2​|∇w|2​ρ​𝑑y=0.\left(\frac{n}{p+1}-\frac{2-n}{2}\right)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}|\nabla w|^{2}\rho dy+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{p+1}\right)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}|y|^{2}|\nabla w|^{2}\rho dy=0. (51)

From (51) and the fact that pp is Sopolev subcritical, it follows that np+1−2−n2>0\frac{n}{p+1}-\frac{2-n}{2}>0 and 12−1p+1>0\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{p+1}>0, hence ∇w≡0\nabla w\equiv 0. This implies that ww is actually a constant. This concludes the proof of Lemma 17. ∎

The second one is due to parabolic estimates:

Lemma 18 (Parabolic estimates).

Let uu be a solution to equation (1). Assume that T=Tmax​(u0)<+∞T=T_{\max}(u_{0})<+\infty and that uu satisfies (20). Then, there is a positive constant CC such that for all t∈[T/2,T)t\in[T/2,T),

‖∇u​(t)‖L∞​(ℝn)≤C​(T−t)−1p−1−12and‖∇2u​(t)‖L∞​(ℝn)≤C​(T−t)−1p−1−1.\|\nabla u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq C(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}-\frac{1}{2}}\quad\text{and}\quad\|\nabla^{2}u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq C(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}-1}. (52)

In similarity variables, we have for all s∈[−log(T/2),+∞)s\in[-\log(T/2),+\infty) and x0∈ℝnx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

‖∇wx0,T​(s)‖L∞​(ℝn)≤Cand‖∇2wx0,T​(s)‖L∞​(ℝn)≤C.\|\nabla w_{x_{0},T}(s)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq C\quad\text{and}\quad\|\nabla^{2}w_{x_{0},T}(s)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq C. (53)
Proof.

Since |h⁡(z)|≤C⁡(|z|p+1)|h(z)|\leq C(|z|^{p}+1) and |h′​(z)|≤C⁡(|z|p−1+1)|h^{\prime}(z)|\leq C(|z|^{p-1}+1) from (3), the proof given in Proposition 23.15, page 189 of Souplet and Quittner [15] in the case h≡0h\equiv 0 extends with no difficulty in this case. ∎

The last one is the nondegeneracy result from Giga and Kohn [6]:

Lemma 19 (Nondegeneracy, Giga and Kohn [6]).

Let p>1p>1, T>0T>0, r>0r>0, σ∈(0,1)\sigma\in(0,1), a∈ℝna\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and denote Qr,σ​(a)=𝐁r​(a)×(T−σ,T)Q_{r,\sigma}(a)=\mathbf{B}_{r}(a)\times(T-\sigma,T). There exists ϵ=ϵ⁡(n,p)>0\epsilon=\epsilon(n,p)>0 such that if uu is a classical solution of

ut−Δ​u=F⁡(u),(x,t)∈Qr,σ​(a),u_{t}-\Delta u=F(u),\quad(x,t)\in Q_{r,\sigma}(a), (54)

where |F⁡(u)|≤M⁡(|u|p+1)|F(u)|\leq M(|u|^{p}+1) for some M>0M>0. Assume that uu satisfies

|u⁡(x,t)|≤ϵ​(T−t)−1p−1,(x,t)∈Qr,σ​(a),|u(x,t)|\leq\epsilon(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}},\quad(x,t)\in Q_{r,\sigma}(a), (55)

then uu is uniformly bounded in a neighborhood of (a,T)(a,T).

Proof.

See Theorem 2.1, page 850 in Giga and Kohn [6]. ∎

Let us now give the proof of Proposition 16.

Proof of Proposition 16.

Consider aa a blow-up point and write ww instead of waw_{a} for simplicity. By Lemma 18 and equation (9), we see that |ws​(y,s)|≤C⁡(|y|+1)|w_{s}(y,s)|\leq C(|y|+1) for some C>0C>0. The proof of Proposition 20 will be very close to that in [3] and [18], thanks to (61) and (62). It happens that the proofs written in Filippas, Kohn, Liu, Herrero and Velázquez [2],[3], [10], [18] in the unperturbed case (h≡0h\equiv 0) hold for equation (60) under the general assumptions (61) and (62). For that reason, we only give the sketch of the proof below and refer to these papers for details of the proofs.
Following [3] and [18], we divide the proof into 3 steps which are given in separated subsections:
- Step 1: deriving the fact that either ‖V+​(s)‖Lρ2+‖V−​(s)‖Lρ2=o⁡(‖Vn​u​l​l​(s)‖Lρ2)\|V_{+}(s)\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}+\|V_{-}(s)\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}=o\left(\|V_{null}(s)\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}\right), or ‖V⁡(s)‖Lρ2=𝒪⁡(e−μ​s)\|V(s)\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}=\mathcal{O}(e^{-\mu s}) for some μ>0\mu>0.
- Step 2: assuming that ‖V⁡(y,s)‖Lρ2∼‖Vn​u​l​l​(y,s)‖Lρ2\|V(y,s)\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}\sim\|V_{null}(y,s)\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}, we find an equation satisfied by Vn​u​l​l​(s)V_{null}(s) as s→+∞s\to+\infty. Solving this equation, we find that ‖V⁡(s)‖Lρ2\|V(s)\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}} behaves like 1s\frac{1}{s} as s→+∞s\to+\infty. Using this information, we can get a more accurate equation for Vn​u​l​l​(s)V_{null}(s) as s→+∞s\to+\infty and then OPENi​i)ii) of Proposition 20 follows.
- Step 3: assuming ‖V⁡(s)‖Lρ2=𝒪⁡(e−μ​s)\|V(s)\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}=\mathcal{O}(e^{-\mu s}) for some μ>0\mu>0 as s→+∞s\to+\infty, we derive OPENi)i) or OPENi​i​i)iii) of Proposition 20.

We give the proof of Theorem 5 in this section. Note that the derivation of Theorem 5 from Theorem 4 in the unperturbed case (h≡0h\equiv 0) was done by Velázquez in [17]. The idea to extend the convergence up to sets of the type {|y|≤K0s}\{|y|\leq K_{0}\sqrt{s}\} or {|y|≤K0e(12−1m)​s}\{|y|\leq K_{0}e^{\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{m}\right)s}\} is to estimate the effect of the convective term −y2⋅∇w-\frac{y}{2}\cdot\nabla w in the equation (9) in LρqL^{q}_{\rho} spaces with q>1q>1. Since the proof of Theorem 5 is actually in spirit by the method given in [17], all that we need to do is to control the strong perturbation term in equation (9). We therefore give the main steps of the proof and focus only on the new arguments. The proof will be separated into two parts: the first part concerns case OPENi​i)ii) in Theorem 4 and gives the asymptotic behavior of ww in the ys\frac{y}{\sqrt{s}} variable, and the second part concerns case OPENi​i​i)iii) in Theorem 4 and gives the asymptotic behavior of ww in the y​e−(12−1m)​sye^{-\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{m}\right)s} variable. In Part 1, we stick to the method of Velázquez [17], whereas, in Part 2, where we work in the scale e−μ​se^{-\mu s} for μ>0\mu>0, we need new ideas to get rid of the term in the scale 1s\frac{1}{s} coming from the strong perturbation.

Appendix A Appendix A

The following lemma shows the asymptotic behavior of the solution of the associated ODE of equation 1:

Lemma A.1.

Let vv be a blow-up solution of the following ordinary differential equation:

v′(t)=vp(t)+h(v),v(T)=+∞for some T>0,v^{\prime}(t)=v^{p}(t)+h(v),\quad v(T)=+\infty\quad\text{for some $T>0$}, (94)

where hh is defined in (3). Then vv satisfies

v⁡(t)∼κ​(T−t)−1p−1as t→T, where κ=(p−1)−1p−1.v(t)\sim\kappa(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\quad\text{as $t\to T$, where $\kappa=(p-1)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}$}.
Proof.

α⁡(s)=−1s+β⁡(s),withβ⁡(s)=𝒪⁡(1s1+σ′),σ′=1−2​σ.\alpha(s)=-\frac{1}{s}+\beta(s),\quad\text{with}\quad\beta(s)=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{1+\sigma^{\prime}}}\right),\quad\sigma^{\prime}=1-2\sigma.

Substituting this into (112) yields

β′​(s)=2​β​(s)s+β2​(s)+𝒪⁡(1s3).\beta^{\prime}(s)=\frac{2\beta(s)}{s}+\beta^{2}(s)+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{3}}\right).

Multiplying this equation by s2s^{2}, we find

[s2​β​(s)]′=s2​β2+𝒪⁡(1s)=𝒪⁡(1s2​σ′)+𝒪⁡(1s).\left[s^{2}\beta(s)\right]^{\prime}=s^{2}\beta^{2}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s}\right)=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{2\sigma^{\prime}}}\right)+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s}\right).

If σ′≥12\sigma^{\prime}\geq\frac{1}{2}, then [s2​β​(s)]′=𝒪⁡(1s)\left[s^{2}\beta(s)\right]^{\prime}=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s}\right) which follows β⁡(s)=𝒪⁡(log⁡ss2)\beta(s)=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\log s}{s^{2}}\right). If σ′<12\sigma^{\prime}<\frac{1}{2}, then β⁡(s)=𝒪⁡(1s1+2​σ′)\beta(s)=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{1+2\sigma^{\prime}}}\right). Using this estimate and repeating the process again, we would obtain β⁡(s)=𝒪⁡(log⁡ss2)\beta(s)=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\log s}{s^{2}}\right) and (114) then follows. Since the argument is similar in the case q∈(2,3)q\in(2,3), we escape here and concludes the proof of Lemma C.2. ∎
